newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa cheerful, brain scan shows no damage.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa cheerful, brain scan shows no damage.

text.p: Mother Teresa was alert and cheerful and her health was stable on Tuesday as she recovered from a fall the previous day, doctors attending to the revered missionary said.
"Mother Teresa's general condition is stable. She is alert and cheerful, there is no neurological deficit and she is being kept under observation," a medical bulletin said.
Doctors attending to the Roman Catholic nun, who is 86, had said earlier in the day that a suspected spot had been found on her brain. But they later said there was no cause for alarm.
"CT (brain) scan results show nothing significant or alarming. We will keep her under observation for two or three days," said Dr. S.K. Sen, medical director at Calcutta's Woodlands Nursing Home.
"But as you know, she always insists on returning home. We may have to release her earlier. Another CT scan will be done within a week," he added.

Doctors said the nun had fallen from a chair on Monday, not from a bed as thought earlier. "She was writing a letter on her desk and when she tried to get up from the chair, she slipped," a nun told Reuters.

The missionary, known as the Saint of the Gutters for her devotion to the poor and destitute, was admitted to the same hospital on August 20 with heart trouble, malaria and pneumonia. She was released 18 days later and told to rest in bed.
"Her condition is stable, but we are going to observe her for some more days," A.K. Bardhan, the hospital's leading heart expert, said earlier in the day.
On Monday, doctors said Mother Teresa continued to have an irregular heart beat, which she has suffered since her stay in the hospital in late August and early September.
"Her cardiac irregularity is still there, but that is nothing alarming," Sen said.
Mother Teresa, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979, was fitted with a cardiac pacemaker in 1989.
In 1991, she was treated at a California hospital for heart disease and bacterial pneumonia. Two years later, she fell in Rome and broke three ribs.
In August 1993, she developed malaria, complicated by heart and lung problems. Last April, she fractured her left collar bone.
The Missionaries of Charity, which she founded in 1949, runs some 544 homes for unwanted children and the destitute in more than 80 cities.
The work includes caring for nearly 7,000 children in 120 homes and arranging 1,500 adoptions each year.
